questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.explanation: 7 has only two factors, 1 and 7, so it is prime.
questions.misconception: 8, 9, and 12 all have extra factors (8: 2 and 4; 9: 3; 12: 2, 3, 4, 6), making them composite.

options: 2 is the only even prime number
No even number is ever prime
questions.explanation: 2 is even and has only the factors 1 and 2, so it is the one and only even prime.
questions.misconception: Odd numbers are not automatically prime — 9 and 21 are odd but composite (9 = 3×3, 21 = 3×7).

questions.prompt: What is the prime factorization of 60?
questions.explanation: 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, and all the factors are prime.
questions.misconception: A prime factorization must end with ALL prime factors — 3 × 4 × 5 has a 4 (composite), and options that stop early are incomplete.

questions.prompt: Why is the number 1 not prime?
options: It has only one factor, but primes need exactly two
It is too small to count
questions.explanation: 1 has only one factor (1 itself), but a prime must have exactly two factors. So 1 is neither prime nor composite.
questions.misconception: 1 is not 'too small' — it fails the definition because it lacks the required second, distinct factor.

questions.prompt: Why is a number like 45 expressed uniquely as primes?
options: 45 = 3 × 3 × 5 is the ONLY way using primes
There are many different prime factorizations
questions.explanation: The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says every number has exactly one prime factorization — 45 is always 3×3×5.
questions.misconception: Factorization might look switchable in order (5×3×3), but as a set of primes the factorization is unique — every path leads to the same primes.
